Turing machine. An abstract mathematical model of computation introduced by Alan Turing in 1936. It consists of an infinite tape, a read-write head, and a finite set of states. It is the foundational model for analyzing what problems are computable, and all major complexity classes like P and NP are defined in terms of Turing machines.

A deterministic Turing machine has a single tape, a read-write head, and a state transition table. This table uniquely determines the next action from the current state and symbol. A nondeterministic Turing machine at each step may follow one of several possible transitions. It accepts an input if any path leads to acceptance.

Turing proved that no algorithm can decide whether an arbitrary Turing machine halts on a given input. The Halting Problem is undecidable. The Church-Turing thesis, formulated in 1936, states that every effectively computable function can be computed by a Turing machine. It is the standard model of computational universality.

Despite simplicity, Turing machines are computationally universal. Any algorithm on any real computer can be simulated by a Turing machine, within a polynomial factor for deterministic machines. The tape is infinite, providing unlimited memory. Most real complexity analysis, however, bounds both time and space.

Formally, P consists of problems decidable by a deterministic Turing machine in polynomial time. NP consists of problems decidable by a nondeterministic Turing machine in polynomial time. These definitions ground the major complexity classes in the Turing machine model.
